onscreen_text.text: Swami, V., Stieger, S., Pietschnig, J., Voracek, M., Furnham, A., & Tovée, M. J. (2012). The influence of facial piercings and observer personality on perceptions of physical attractiveness and intelligence. European Psychologist, 17(3), 213–221.
Martino, S. (2008). Perceptions of a photograph of a woman with visible piercings. Psychological Reports, 103(1), 134–138.

transcript.text: Were your parents right when they said that face piercings would ruin your attractiveness?
Well, there's actually some research on this.
Swami and colleagues had raters assess the same male face carrying no piercing, a single piercing, and then several.
A single piercing was already enough to drop perceived attractiveness by over a whole point.
What's even more notable is that perceived intelligence declined alongside it.
And the more piercings, the lower both ratings went.
Interestingly, this is different for women.
The same first female model cost less than half as much in attractiveness ratings.
So facial piercings seem to transgress fewer expectations on a woman.
But there is a bit more nuance to all of this.
Psychologist Sara Martino scored a photograph of a woman across 13 traits, pierced and unpierced.
And her raters called the pierced version less religious, but more creative, more artistic, and more mysterious.
Which is roughly what people get pierced for.
It is probably why a nose ring reads as cool on Lenny Kravitz and as a liability on your LinkedIn headshot.
If you want us to analyze your face, click the link in bio at Qoves.com.

narrative_arc: Hook questioning traditional views on facial piercings using celebrity edits.
Presentation of academic study data showing negative impacts on male attractiveness and perceived intelligence.
Gender comparison showing a smaller negative impact on female attractiveness ratings.
Nuanced counter-analysis showing positive associations with creativity, artistic flair, and mystery.
Contextual conclusion contrasting artistic icon perception vs corporate headshot standards.
Call to action for custom facial analysis software.

cta.what: Prompting viewers to get their face analyzed by visiting the link in bio at Qoves.com.
